en: Itivuttaka 94: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a wooden post, and the person who is like a tree stump. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. This, monks, is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a wooden post? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. But he does not harbor that hatred for long; soon he becomes free from it. This, monks, is called a person like a wooden post. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree stump? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. He harbors that hatred for a long time; he does not become free from it. This, monks, is called a person like a tree stump. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Venerable Ānanda, what is the meaning of ‘a person like a stone pillar,’ ‘a person like a wooden post,’ and ‘a person like a tree stump’? “Friend, just as a stone pillar is fixed, immovable, and unshakable, so too, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. He harbors that hatred for a long time; he does not become free from it. This, friend, is called a person like a stone pillar. Just as a wooden post, though it may be struck by the wind, eventually returns to its original state, so too, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. But he does not harbor that hatred for long; soon he becomes free from it. This, friend, is called a person like a wooden post. Just as a tree stump, once cut down, remains standing for a long time, so too, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hatred toward his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, his companions, his kinsmen, and his relatives. He harbors that hatred for a long time; he does not become free from it. This, friend, is called a person like a tree stump. Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda. Delighted, that monk rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda. Thus it was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard. End of the fifth chapter of the third collection. Thus it was said. 94. Thus it was said by the Blessed One; so have I heard:

"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should investigate in such a way that, as he investigates, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, nor settled internally, and being without clinging, he does not tremble."

“Bhikkhus, when consciousness is not distracted and not scattered externally, and is not settled internally, for one who does not cling and is not agitated, there is no origination of the arising of suffering—of birth, aging, and death—in the future.
Thus spoke the Blessed One. With reference to this, it is said:
“For the bhikkhu who has abandoned the seven attachments and whose guide has been severed,
the wandering through births is exhausted.”
“There is no further becoming for him.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
